summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Suriname since 1869, for men and women, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Article 302 of the 1910 Penal Code, which had set 18 for same-sex acts, was amended in 2015 to remove the difference.

Suriname has no statutory procedure for changing a gender marker, and trans people have obtained recognition only through litigation. On 11 January 2017 the Kantongerecht in the Eerste Kanton ordered the civil registrar to record a post-operative trans woman as female by marginal note, holding that the conflict between her socio-psychological gender role and her birth registration breached the right to respect for private life under Article 17 of the Constitution, Article 17 of the ICCPR and Article 11 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The court found that Suriname law provided no statutory procedure for a transsexual gender-marker change and interpreted Articles 17 and 64-67a of the Civil Code under Articles 106 and 137 of the Constitution to reach that result. The applicant had undergone male-to-female surgery on 22 April 2009 and obtained a forename change on 12 January 2011. The Central Bureau of Civil Affairs appealed in February 2017. On 21 January 2022 the Hof van Justitie ruled in her favour and ordered the change recorded on her birth certificate, establishing a precedent for amending sex and name in official registers. Execution of that judgment through the Ministry of Interior Affairs was still being sought, and legislation permitting change without prolonged litigation was still absent.

On 31 January 2023 the Constitutional Court described the Civil Code as very outdated, out of step with contemporary developments and urgently requiring amendment, in a case referencing the same transgender applicant.

Anti-discrimination law names sexual orientation expressly in several instruments. In March 2015 Articles 175, 175a and 176 of the Penal Code were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. Articles 176c and 500a forbid discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation in employment and in the provision of goods and services. The Employment Equal Treatment Act 2022 extended workplace protection to gender identity for the first time. Whether Articles 175, 175a and 176 reach gender identity is not stated in the sources available here.

Constitutional protection is implicit rather than enumerated. Article 8.2 lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government reads that clause as covering sexual orientation and gender identity, but no statute lists either as a protected ground. A July 2024 civil-society report from Projekta Foundation with VIDS and the LGBT Platform recommended a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

Partner recognition is unresolved. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised in law. On 13 February 2025 Judge Shanti Bikhari ruled that the provisions used to refuse same-sex marriage conflict with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the American Convention on Human Rights, ordered the state to amend the relevant laws and required the Bureau of Civil Affairs to register the marriages; the ruling may still be overturned. In February 2023 the Constitutional Court had held that the ban did not violate the constitution or Suriname's obligations under the American Convention, while finding the Civil Code outdated and in need of modernisation. Suriname is bound by the January 2018 judgment of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights holding that same-sex marriage is a right protected by the American Convention.

Enforcement and social conditions lag the legal position. A submission to the UN Human Rights Committee from the LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata records that LGBTI people still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation despite constitutional protection. The US State Department's 2015 human rights report for Suriname likewise records discrimination against LGBTI persons. At the Human Rights Committee's July 2024 review of Suriname, the state said its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation and pointed to monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while committee experts pressed on implementation of the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The LGBT Platform Suriname reports that it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

When the first-instance court granted a gender-marker change in 2017, the Association of Pentecostal Churches in Suriname and the Suriname Islamic Association, which had opposed recognition of gender change, indicated they would accept the verdict; the Central Bureau of Civil Affairs appealed the ruling the following month.

LGBTI organisations are able to register in Suriname.
localsOnly:
Workplace discrimination on the ground of gender identity is prohibited under the Employment Equal Treatment Act 2022, the first time gender identity has been named in a protective statute.

Changing a gender marker requires litigation. The 2017 first-instance judgment and the 2022 appellate judgment in the same case supply the working route, and the applicant in that case had undergone surgery in 2009. No self-determination procedure exists, and the 2022 judgment's execution through the Ministry of Interior Affairs was still being pursued.

The Constitutional Court's January 2023 finding that the Civil Code is outdated and urgently requires amendment leaves the statutory position open.

The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded on 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action, and has sought a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.
